lesson.title: The Sentences a Computer Can Judge True or False
lesson.summary: A boolean expression is any expression that evaluates to exactly one of two values, True or False, giving programs a precise way to represent yes-or-no facts.
lesson.body:
Every expression in Python produces a value, and that value has a type. An arithmetic expression such as 3 + 4 produces an integer. A boolean expression is different from an arithmetic one only in what type of value it always produces: no matter how the expression is written, it reduces to exactly one of two possible values, the built-in constants True and False. This is the boolean type, and it exists because so many real questions a program needs to answer are naturally two valued. Is the user logged in? Is the shopping cart empty? Has the password been typed correctly? Each of these is really asking for a single True or False answer, and boolean expressions are the tool Python gives you to compute that answer.

The simplest possible boolean expressions are the literals True and False themselves, typed directly into code. Nearly everything else you will write is a boolean expression built by combining other values with operators that Python defines to return a boolean result. Comparison operators such as ==, !=, <, and >= compare two values and produce True or False. Logical operators such as and, or, and not combine or invert existing boolean values to produce a new one. Both families are covered in depth later in this chapter, but the key idea to hold onto now is that Python evaluates all of them the same way it evaluates an arithmetic expression: it works through the values and operators present, applies each operator's own rule, and collapses the whole thing down to a single result.

Trace this short program line by line:

age = 15
is_teen = age >= 13 and age <= 19
print(is_teen)

Python evaluates age >= 13 first, substituting the value 15 for age, which gives 15 >= 13, a True result. It then evaluates age <= 19 the same way, giving 15 <= 19, also True. The and operator combines these two boolean values, and since both sides are True, the whole expression evaluates to True. That single value, not the arithmetic or the individual comparisons, is what gets stored in is_teen. Printing is_teen displays True.

This distinction matters enormously once you reach control flow. An if statement in Python does not check whether a variable holds a number or a string; it checks whether a boolean expression evaluates to True, and it runs the indented block only in that case. A while loop repeats its body for exactly as long as its boolean expression keeps evaluating to True. Neither structure would work if conditions could produce anything other than a clean, unambiguous True or False. Boolean expressions are what make that guarantee possible, and every conditional or loop you write from here forward depends on reducing some real world condition down to one of these two values.

It is also worth noticing that a boolean expression can be assigned to a variable exactly like any other value, and that variable can then be reused anywhere a boolean expression is expected, including inside another boolean expression. A common but slightly redundant pattern beginners write is something like if is_teen == True:, comparing a boolean variable to the literal True. Since is_teen already holds True or False directly, comparing it to True produces the very same value it already held; writing if is_teen: says the same thing more directly, and is considered better style once truthiness, covered later in this chapter, makes clear exactly why that shortcut works.
